newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian car industry at the crossroads.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian car industry at the crossroads.

text.p: The Australian car industry is at a crossroads, with the four manufacturers currently investing more than A$4 billion in local plants and models but nervously awaiting government response to a critical industry review.
Ford Motor Co and General Motors Corp both have warned they may pull out of Australia if the federal government slashes tariffs on imported cars.

According to Mitsubishi Motors Australia Ltd (MMAL), the future of the industry in Australia will depend on investor perceptions of government commitment to assistance - chiefly tariff levels, export support, and microeconomic reform.

Mitsubishi told a Productivity Commission review that the outstanding feature of the Australian car market was the lack of any significant growth over the past 20 years, with the "remarkably low propensity" by Australians to buy new cars.
Recently released figures show Australian new vehicle sales rose 1.2 percent to 650,000 in 1996 from 1995, but the industry says sales are expected to fall three percent in 1997.

The Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries (FCAI), the main industry body, says sales should be closer to 700,000 units, but remain at 1980s levels despite a 20 percent rise in population over the period.

"Because of the taxes we have on cars ... because our wharves are highly inefficient, and a whole range of other things, we will probably finish with 630,000 next year," FCAI executive Terry Pennington told Reuters.
The FCAI says there are few hopes for any major boost in the short-term and that competition will intensify with cheaper imported cars which made up 46.4 percent of local sales in 1996.

The debate on government assistance comes after a year of mixed fortunes for the country's four car manufacturers with GM's local unit, General Motors-Holden's, and Ford Australia announcing record profits against large losses for yen sensitive Mitsubishi and Toyota Motor Corp.

FCAI figures show domestic vehicle production declined from 377,000 units in 1985 to an unofficial 323,000 in 1996, with the number of manufacturers dropping from five to four and the number of models from 13 to five in the last decade.
"The industry has a critical mass of 80,000-100,000 units per manufacturer ... and recent volumes have been well below this level," Ford said in its submission to the review.
So carmakers are looking offshore, saying access to markets in Asia Pacific is fundamental to a viable domestic industry.

"There are some markets, for example Korea, where it is virtually impossible to get into," Mitsubishi spokesman Kevin Taylor told Reuters. "Australia is probably one of the most open motor markets in this part of the world and we have no problems with (competition) provided it is a level playing field."
The FCAI said while official 1996 export figures are not yet finalised, they could rise to A$1.85 billion from A$1.65 billion in 1995, with a late-year boost by Toyota and Mitsubishi cars.
Toyota has said Australian manufacturers' exports could rise to A$3 billion by the year 2000 but it warned rising global competition could undermine that prediction.
Benefiting from the new global approach of their corporate parents, Holden and Mitsubishi have made heavy investments in models aimed at export markets.

Holden, which has announced a A$1.4 billion investment programme over five years, is to become the Asian regional source for one of the mainstream General Motors models with its new Vectra, to reach production of 50,000 units a year.

Mitsubishi last year launched a new engine, which will supply its parent company in Japan, and global production for a new Magna sedan, with planned exports of 25,000 units a year, following a A$525 million investment.

Toyota has spent A$420 million on a new plant, part of A$1.2 billion it says it is investing to 2000, with exports aimed to reach A$600 million a year by then, while Ford is to produce a new Falcon model for the local market with a total new investment of A$1 billion.
But the industry has warned investment levels depend on ongoing federal government support for the industry.
Under the current government car plan, tariffs, now at 25 percent, will drop to 15 percent by the year 2000, having been cut 2.5 percent a year from 52 percent a decade ago.
The Productivity Commission is urging a further radical cut in tariffs to five percent by 2004.

Critics, disappointed at the rejection of industry calls for a moratorium on further cuts until South East Asian nations reciprocate, have warned of plant closures, massive job losses, and the end of the domestic industry.

In calling for microeconomic reform, the industry is arguing it has borne the pain of significant productivity changes in the last decade and the government must now examine critical issues such as the labour market and sales tax.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
